Hawaiʻi Appleseed Center for Law & Economic Justice

Keeping Hawaiʻi's Families Out of Poverty

How federal and state tax credits lift tens of thousands of local residents above the poverty line — and what expanding them would do. Tax year 2025.

Executive Summary

The combined impact of federal & state tax credits

34,539
People kept out of poverty every year by the federal EITC, federal CTC, and Hawaiʻi state EITC
$132M
Annual poverty gap closed by the three credits combined
+6,733
Additional people who would be lifted if Hawaiʻi enacted a $650-per-child state CTC

Tax credits give working Hawaiʻi families the money they need for food, rent, and medical care — without the application overhead of programs like SNAP. This dashboard reports the modeled anti-poverty impact of every major federal and state credit, broken down by county and legislative district.

At the headline level, the federal EITC alone lifts roughly 20,457 Hawaiʻi residents out of poverty each year; the federal CTC adds 16,669; and Hawaiʻi's 40%-of-federal state EITC contributes another 9,838. The three together close a $132M annual poverty gap.

Section 1

Supplemental Poverty Measure rates by county

The Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM) is a more complete picture of poverty than the official measure — it counts the value of food, housing, and medical benefits as resources, and subtracts out-of-pocket medical, child care, and work expenses. Hawaiʻi's high cost of living drives a higher threshold than the contiguous-US baseline.

What if Hawaiʻi expanded its credits?

Two policy proposals modeled: raising Hawaiʻi's state EITC from its current 40% of the federal credit to 100%, and creating a new $650-per-qualifying-child state CTC (refundable). Cost estimates are from legislative analysis.

PolicyAdditional people liftedAdditional gap closedEst. annual cost

$650/child HI state CTC 6,733 $15M ~$83M (legislative est.)
Both combined 17,596 (non-additive — see methodology) $39M ~$113M
Section 5

Single-parent household poverty & RxKids Hawaiʻi

31.9%
Single-parent household poverty rate (TY 2025)
14,231
People in single-parent households living below the SPM threshold
6,431
Single-parent persons lifted by federal EITC, CTC, and HI EITC combined

Head-of-household tax units serve as the closest PUMS proxy for single-parent households — primarily single mothers in Hawaiʻi. The combined federal + state credit stack reduces single-parent poverty by 45% of the baseline persons-in-poverty count. Hypothetical policy expansions could push this further:

  • Raising HI EITC from 40% → 100% of federal: +1,043 additional single-parent persons lifted
  • New $650/child HI state CTC: +655 additional single-parent persons lifted

A modeled RxKids Hawaiʻi program (prenatal + postnatal cash prescriptions for Medicaid-enrolled families) is in scope as a Tier 4 follow-up; see RXKIDS_METHODOLOGY.md. RxKids-specific lift numbers will appear here when the scenario is wired into the production report.

Section 6

Methodology & data sources

What is the Supplemental Poverty Measure?

Unlike the official poverty measure, the SPM accounts for in-kind benefits (SNAP, housing assistance, school lunch), tax credits (EITC, CTC), and subtracts non-discretionary expenses (medical out-of-pocket, child care, work expenses, taxes). Hawaiʻi's SPM threshold is adjusted upward for the Honolulu Median Rent Index applied to the housing share of the threshold. Source: Census Bureau P60-280/283; Burns & Fox 2021 SEHSD WP21-17.

Data sources
  • Microdata: US Census Bureau 5-year ACS PUMS 2018-2022, Hawaiʻi sample
  • Tax credit calibration: IRS SOI ZIP-code data, TY 2022 Hawaiʻi anchors
  • SNAP / WIC / LIHEAP take-up: USDA-FNS and HI DHS BESSD administrative caseloads
  • MOOP / childcare / work expense: CPS ASEC Hawaiʻi donor records
  • Equivalence scale: Census Betson 3-parameter (Burns & Fox 2021)
  • Geographic adjustment: Honolulu MSA Median Rent Index applied to per-tenure housing share
Known limitations
  • Static counterfactual: no modeled labor supply / marriage / fertility / filing response
  • Unit of analysis: SPM unit (per Census P60-280). Tax-unit-grained calculations are also available via --by-tax-unit for diagnostic comparisons.
  • District assignment: within-PUMA HD/SD via deterministic SERIALNO hash; ±20% point-estimate uncertainty until IRS SOI ZIP raking enabled
  • Marginal attribution is non-additive: sum of single-credit lifts ≠ combined-credit lift due to phase-out interactions

Source: U.S. Census Bureau 5-Year ACS PUMS 2018-2022; Census-Forecaster tax simulation model, Hawaiʻi Appleseed 2026. Generated from poverty_impact_2025_tier4_spm. Source code.
